svg.aria-label: Diagram: what Amazon Security Lake converts, what a subscriber actually receives under each of its two access types, and what the OCSF version tables imply for queries. Security Lake is a fully managed security data lake service used to centralize security data from AWS environments, SaaS providers, on premises, cloud sources and third-party sources into a purpose-built data lake stored in the customer's own AWS account, backed by Amazon S3 buckets with the customer retaining ownership of the data, and with one bucket per AWS Region. It converts ingested data into Apache Parquet format and the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework, or OCSF, automatically partitioning incoming data from natively supported AWS services. Two distinct transformations happen and only one is the schema: partitioning and Parquet conversion give columnar storage and partition pruning, which is what makes queries cheap, while the OCSF transformation gives field names that mean the same thing across sources, which is what makes queries joinable. The crucial qualifier, repeated in the documentation, is that automatic conversion to OCSF applies to natively-supported AWS services only: logs and events written from custom sources must themselves already adhere to the OCSF schema and to Apache Parquet format, so the transformation work for non-AWS sources sits upstream with the customer and Security Lake validates shape rather than translating. On the schema itself, OCSF provides a standard schema for common security events and explicitly defines versioning criteria to facilitate schema evolution, and AWS publishes the source identification mapping twice: a Version 1 table at metadata version 1.0.0-rc.2 and a Version 2 table at 1.1.0. Most rows agree between them but the Security Hub CSPM row does not: in Version 1 its class_name is Security Finding, while in Version 2 the class_name is Vulnerability Finding, Compliance Finding, or Detection Finding, and its product and vendor fields change from fixed strings to values matching the AWS Security Finding Format. One class became three, so a dashboard or query filtering on class_name equals Security Finding was correct when written and matches nothing against Version 2 data, and SQL does not warn that a predicate stopped matching because an empty result set is a valid answer to a well-formed query. Other mappings are recorded for reference: VPC Flow Logs map to class_name Network Activity, Route 53 Resolver Query Logs to DNS Activity, and CloudTrail Management Events to API Activity, Authentication, or Account Change, which means one source already maps to three classes before any version change. A further subtlety is that OCSF is a convention on read rather than an enforcement: subscribers can treat the logs and events as generic Parquet records, or apply the OCSF schema event class to more accurately interpret the information in a record, so a reader working positionally gets data while a reader applying the event class gets meaning, and only the latter notices when a class changes underneath it. On consumption, the word subscriber covers two materially different grants distinguished by the accessTypes parameter of the CreateSubscriber API. The S3 access type gives data access: subscribers are notified of new objects as data is written to the S3 bucket, by default through an HTTPS endpoint that the subscriber provides or alternatively by polling an Amazon SQS queue, and those subscribers directly access the S3 objects themselves. The LAKEFORMATION access type gives query access: subscribers directly query AWS Lake Formation tables in the customer's S3 bucket using services like Amazon Athena, which is the primary query engine, though Amazon Redshift Spectrum and Spark SQL also work because they integrate with the AWS Glue Data Catalog. The difference determines what can be withheld, because a Parquet object contains every column of every record within it so handing one over hands over all of it, whereas a Lake Formation table is the layer at which column-level and row-level controls can be expressed. Both are called subscribers and only the second provides anywhere to say that a given team sees only certain fields. Across both types, subscribers may consume data only from the sources and in the AWS Regions that the customer specifies, and Security Lake automatically creates and exchanges the credentials needed between Security Lake and the subscriber, which removes a common source of misconfiguration in cross-account log bucket sharing. Finally, rollup Regions can be designated to consolidate security log and event data from multiple Regions, which AWS notes can help comply with data residency compliance requirements, though the same consolidation that satisfies one residency regime deliberately moves security data across a Regional boundary and may breach another.
svg.title: A standard schema with versions: the query that was correct when written returns nothing
svg.text: One schema, two versions, and SQL does not warn you.
Amazon Security Lake — what gets converted, who can read it, and what pins a query.
Two transformations, and only one of them is the schema
Parquet + partitioning → columnar storage, partition pruning. This is what makes the queries cheap. Durable.
OCSF → field names meaning the same thing across sources. This is what makes the queries joinable.
And it is the half with a version number on it.
AWS publishes the mapping twice. One row disagrees, and it is the one carrying your findings.
Security Hub CSPM v1 (1.0.0-rc.2) class_name = “Security Finding”
v2 (1.1.0) class_name = “Vulnerability Finding, Compliance
Finding, or Detection Finding”
One class became three. A dashboard filtering the old value was correct when written and now matches nothing.
SQL does not warn that a predicate stopped matching. An empty result is a valid answer to a well-formed query.
accessTypes = S3
“Subscribers can directly access the S3 objects
and receive notifications of new objects”
via an HTTPS endpoint they provide, or by polling SQS
A Parquet object carries every column of every
record in it. Handing one over hands over all of it.
Nowhere to say “this team sees these fields”.
accessTypes = LAKEFORMATION
“directly query AWS Lake Formation tables in your
S3 bucket with services like Amazon Athena”
also Redshift Spectrum, Spark SQL — via Glue Catalog
A table is the layer where column- and row-level
controls can be expressed.
Default to this. Reach for S3 only when raw files are needed.
vs
The qualifier that is easy to read past
“converts logs and events that come from natively-supported AWS services” — and for everything else:
custom sources “must adhere to the OCSF schema and an Apache Parquet format”. That work is yours, upstream.
OCSF is opt-in on read
“treat the logs as generic Parquet records or apply the
OCSF schema event class”
Read positionally and you get data. Apply the class and you get meaning.
One source already maps to three classes
CloudTrail Mgmt → API Activity | Authentication |
Account Change
So “one source, one class” was never true. v2 just spread it further.
Good defaults worth keeping: subscribers consume “only from the sources, and in the AWS Regions, that you specify”, and Security Lake
“automatically creates and exchanges the credentials” — which removes the wildcard-bucket-policy failure entirely.
Alert when a saved query drops to zero rows. For security data, an unexplained zero is the signal.
OCSF “defines versioning criteria to facilitate schema evolution” — evolution is a feature, and your queries are pinned to it.
